examples: Do not honk in a hospital zone.
The cab behind us honked twice.
Someone has been honking at that stalled van for a minute.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (honk the horn), intransitive (the taxi honked at me)

entries.meaning: To keep moving without power, using only momentum or the slope. ---
examples: Take your foot off the gas and coast to the sign.
The truck coasted the last half mile on empty.
We were coasting downhill with the engine off.

entries.meaning: To run an engine while the vehicle is not moving. ---
examples: Diesel engines idle louder than gas engines.
The bus idled at the curb for ten minutes.
A sign asks drivers to stop idling near the school.
entries.русский: работать на холостом ходу; держать двигатель включённым
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (do not idle your engine), intransitive (the bus idled at the curb)
entries.contrast: Sounds like idol; the silent -e drops before -ing: idling.

entries.meaning: To make an engine turn faster and louder. ---
examples: Do not rev a cold engine.
The kid next to us revved his motor at every light.
Someone has been revving a dirt bike since six.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rev the engine), intransitive (the motor revved)
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the v doubles: revved, revving.

entries.meaning: To drive too close behind another vehicle. ---
examples: Please do not tailgate on an icy road.
A pickup tailgated us for ten miles.
He rear-ended her because he was tailgating.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tailgate the car ahead), intransitive (stop tailgating)

entries.meaning: To move more slowly, or to make something move more slowly. ---
examples: Rain will slow the whole delivery route.
Traffic slowed to a crawl near the tunnel.
The train was slowing as it entered the yard.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (slow the truck), intransitive (traffic slowed)

entries.meaning: To make an engine begin to run, or to begin to run. ---
examples: Start the car and let it warm up.
The van started on the third try.
It has not started once since the cold snap.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (start the engine), intransitive (the truck would not start)

entries.meaning: To move a vehicle carefully into or through a tight place. ---
examples: It takes practice to maneuver a long trailer.
She maneuvered the forklift between two pallets.
He was maneuvering out of the space when the mirror caught.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (maneuver the trailer), intransitive (maneuver around the crates)

entries.meaning: To take a different route because the usual one is closed. ---
examples: We can detour around the closed bridge.
The truck detoured through two small towns.
Traffic has been detoured onto a county road.
entries.русский: ехать в объезд, объезжать, делать крюк
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they detoured the traffic), intransitive (we detoured through town)

entries.meaning: To put more fuel into a vehicle. ---
examples: We can refuel at the next truck stop.
The crew refueled the plane in twenty minutes.
The ferry was refueling when we boarded.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (refuel the plane), intransitive (we refueled in Reno)
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one l: refueled, refueling (British refuelled, refuelling).

entries.meaning: To fill something with air until it is firm. ---
examples: Inflate the tires to thirty-five pounds.
He inflated the spare before the trip.
The airbag had already inflated when help arrived.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (inflate the tires), intransitive (the airbag inflates instantly)

examples: Do not bump the car in front while parking.
She bumped the mirror on the garage door.
The truck was bumping over the rail crossing.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (bump the car ahead), intransitive (we bumped along the dirt road)
entries.contrast: You bump into something you did not mean to hit.

entries.meaning: To put something away neatly in a space made for it. ---
examples: Please stow your bag under the seat.
He stowed the straps in the side box.
All the gear has been stowed below deck.
entries.contrast: Rhymes with go, not with cow: /stoʊ/.

entries.meaning: To attach a trailer to a vehicle that will pull it. ---
examples: Hitch the trailer and check the lights.
He hitched the boat to his pickup.
The camper was hitched to an old van.
entries.contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: hitches.

entries.meaning: To send a vehicle, person, or shipment out to a destination. ---
examples: They dispatch trucks every two hours.
The office dispatched a tow truck within minutes.
Two vans have been dispatched to the warehouse.

entries.meaning: To pay a company so that it will cover the cost if something is lost or damaged. ---
examples: You can insure the package for its full value.
He insured the truck before the first haul.
The cargo was insured against water damage.

entries.meaning: To move slowly along the ground, said of an airplane. ---
examples: Planes taxi to the far end of the runway.
We taxied for twenty minutes before takeoff.
The jet was still taxiing when the crew stood up.
entries.contrast: Odd forms: taxis, taxied, but taxiing keeps both is.

entries.meaning: To call to a taxi or driver to stop for you. ---
examples: It is hard to hail a cab in the rain.
He hailed a taxi outside the station.
She was hailing a cab with one arm and holding her bag with the other.

entries.meaning: To share one car with other people for a regular trip.
examples: Three of us carpool to the plant.
They carpooled all through college.
We have been carpooling since gas went up.
entries.русский: ездить вместе на одной машине (по очереди)
